  How a fit was computed, the Monte Carlo samples behind it, and the
  uncertainty of its estimates from profile likelihoods and the parametric

---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "90%",
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)
# The profiles and the bootstrap take a few minutes, so precompute.R computes
# them once, with the code shown below, and the article loads the results.
precomputed <- readRDS("precomputed/checking-a-fit.rds")
```

Two questions follow every fit. Was the fit computed reliably, and how
uncertain are its estimates? This article answers the first with
`check_fit()` and the Monte Carlo samples, and the second with profile
likelihoods and the parametric bootstrap. Whether the model suits the data is a
different question, which the article *Assessing predictions and simulations*
takes up.

## A fit to check

The model is a binomial model of river blindness in 90 Liberian villages, with
the logarithm of elevation as a covariate and a spatial Gaussian process.

```{r fit-model, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)

data(liberia)
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, propose_crs(liberia, messages = FALSE))

set.seed(2026)
fit <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
             data = liberia,
             family = "binomial",
             denominator = ntest)
fit
```

## How the fit was computed

Binomial, Poisson and negative binomial models are fitted by Monte Carlo
maximum likelihood. The likelihood is an integral over the spatial effects at
the villages, which RiskMap estimates by importance sampling. The estimate is
then certified with an independent sample, which bounds its Monte Carlo error
in statistical standard errors. `check_fit()` goes through this computation.

```{r check-fit}
checks <- check_fit(fit)
checks
```

Each row is one check. *Monte Carlo accuracy* is the bound on the Monte Carlo
error, here a small fraction of a standard error. *Importance weights* gives the
effective number of draws and the shape of the tail of the weights, which
should stay below 0.7. *Other maxima* says whether a search found a higher
maximum of the likelihood. The remaining rows flag variances estimated at zero,
a spatial scale too short for the spacing of the data, and the importance
distribution used. A check that needs attention is marked with an exclamation
mark or a cross, and the fix follows. `summary()` gives the evidence behind
each row, and `plot()` draws the certificate, the effective draws and the tail
shape at each stage of the fit, and the screen of short spatial scales behind
the check for other maxima.

```{r check-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5, out.width = "100%"}
plot(checks)
```

The extra checks compute something new. The check of the radius predicts how
often the allowance in the certificate for the Monte Carlo error of the
certification sample is too small. It takes about twice as long as the fit.

```{r check-radius}
check_fit(fit, extra = "radius")
```

## The samples of the spatial effects

After the fit, a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler draws the spatial effects at
the villages given the data, at the estimated parameters. `predict()` uses
these samples. `plot_mcmc()` shows the trace and autocorrelation of the mean
of the effects and of the effect at the village with the smallest effective
sample size, and the effective sample sizes at all villages, which
`summarise_mcmc()` returns.

```{r mcmc-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot_mcmc(fit)
```

```{r mcmc-summary}
summary(summarise_mcmc(fit)$ess)
```

## Profile likelihoods

`summary()` gives Wald intervals, which assume that the estimate is normally
distributed. That is often poor for the spatial variance and scale, whose
likelihood is skewed. A profile likelihood maximises the likelihood over the
other parameters at each value of one, and the values where it falls by
$\chi^2_{1,0.95}/2$ from its maximum give a 95% interval. For a binomial model
the likelihood is estimated from one bank of Monte Carlo draws.

```{r profile, eval = FALSE}
profiles <- profile(fit,
                    parameters = c("log_elevation", "sigma2", "phi"),
                    pairs = list(c("sigma2", "phi")),
                    cores = 4)
```

```{r profile-load, include = FALSE}
profiles <- precomputed$profiles
```

```{r profile-print}
profiles
```

The profile interval of the scale stretches much further above the estimate
than the Wald interval. `plot()` draws each profile with its interval, the
dashed curve being the quadratic approximation behind the Wald interval, and
the joint profile of the spatial variance and scale with their profiles along
its sides. `plot_profile()` selects parameters and pairs, and
`scale = "deviance"` draws the profile deviance instead.

```{r profile-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7.5, out.width = "100%"}
plot(profiles)
```

`check_fit()` reads the profiles too. It flags a profile that is flat, so that
an interval is open at one end, or that rises above the estimate, which would
mean the fit had not found the maximum.

```{r check-profile}
check_fit(fit, profile = profiles)
```

## The parametric bootstrap

The parametric bootstrap simulates datasets from the fitted model at its
estimate, refits the model to each, and uses the spread of the estimates.
It gives bias-corrected (BC) intervals as well as percentile intervals.

```{r bootstrap, eval = FALSE}
bootstrap <- parametric_bootstrap(fit,
                                  n_sim = 200,
                                  cores = 4)
```

```{r bootstrap-load, include = FALSE}
bootstrap <- precomputed$bootstrap
```

```{r bootstrap-summary}
summary(bootstrap)
```

```{r bootstrap-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "100%"}
plot_bootstrap(bootstrap, log_scale = TRUE)
```

The bootstrap distribution of the scale is wide and skewed, as the profile
showed. Some simulated datasets carry little information about it, and give
estimates near zero, which pull the lower percentile limit down. The
bias-corrected interval adjusts for this, and is closer to the profile
interval.

## Learn more

Chapter [3](https://www.mbgr.org/03_model-fitting.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treats the
estimation of geostatistical models, including Monte Carlo maximum likelihood
and the uncertainty of the estimates.
